events.headline: AI bubble burst ‘inevitable’, India-US trade ties strained by Lindsey Graham bill, says Finance Ministry report

items.title: AI bubble burst ‘inevitable’, India-US trade ties strained by Lindsey Graham bill, says Finance Ministry report
items.summary: India’s Finance Ministry says trade ties with the US are strained after the Lindsey Graham Bill, allowing tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian crude. The report also warns of higher oil prices, bond yields, slower capital flows and an eventual AI investment slowdown.

events.article_text:
India's finance ministry has said that trade relations with the United States are currently strained because of the passage of the Lindsey Graham Bill through the US Congress and the presidential approval of the same, as per the Monthy Economic Report published on Thursday.

The bill empowers the US president to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries that purchase Russian crude oil, with India and China being among them.

The report comes at a time when the world economy is reeling under the effects of the US-Iran war, with oil prices having spiked in September. On the other hand, global bonds yeilds are higher, and will be spilling over into India's domestic bond yields. It also says that cross-border capital flow will slow down as higher interest rates will persuade investors to continue remain invested in domestic markets as global uncertainty rises.t

"Sustained high quality, consistent and reasonably swift decision-making will reassure investors. More importantly, India must work on ensuring that the economy is more competition-friendly rather than business-friendly. Only a competitive economy will become a successful, innovative, and manufacturing economy. Improved governance and enhanced state capacity at all levels of the government hold the key to a competitive Indian economy," the report said.

It also highlighted that India's growth momentum has held on amid the heightened global uncertainties. "The escalation of tensions in West Asia disrupted energy markets and trade routes, adding to uncertainty in an already uneven global economy. Domestic activity, nevertheless, remained firm, supported by strong domestic consumption and sustained investment," it said.

Retail inflation rose to 4.82% in August, while food inflation stood at 5.95%. Wholesale inflation accelerated to 9.92%, driven in part by renewed fuel and power price pressures.

India's external sector remained resilient, supported by services exports, remittances, forex reserves and capital inflows, the report said. Foreign-exchange reserves stood at $765.9 billion as of Sept. 18, providing import cover of about 11.1 months.

The finance ministry report also says that the AI bubble has not yet begun its inevitable meaningful deflation, which is driving capital investment and capital flows out of the country.

It says that developing countries, like India, are racing to secure investments to finance their manufacturing aspirations at a time when global supply chains are being weaponised. "Thus, India, as do other developing nations, faces a stiff challenge to attract capital flows," the report states.

the_story: India's finance ministry reported that trade ties with the US are strained because of the Lindsey Graham Bill, which allows the US president to put tariffs (taxes on imports) of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil, like India and China.
The world economy is struggling with a US-Iran war that spiked oil prices in September, while global bond yields (the interest rates governments pay to borrow money) are climbing.
Retail inflation (how fast everyday prices rise for consumers) hit 4.82% in August, with food inflation at 5.95% and wholesale inflation at 9.92% driven by fuel and power costs.
India's foreign-exchange reserves (the country's stash of foreign currencies and gold) stood at $765.9 billion as of September 18, enough to cover 11.1 months of imports.
The report also warned that an inevitable bursting of the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble is drawing capital investments away from developing countries like India.
analysis.what_happened: India's finance ministry published its Monthly Economic Report, warning that trade ties with the US are strained due to a new US bill targeting countries that buy Russian oil. At the same time, global conflicts in West Asia have spiked oil prices, and rising global interest rates are making it harder for developing nations like India to attract foreign investments.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local grocery shop facing higher wholesale prices from suppliers because of neighbourhood fights, while customers demand lower prices and money becomes tighter to borrow.
why_it_matters_india: The US bill threatens up to 100% tariffs on countries buying Russian crude oil, creating trade friction -> Indian refiners face potential hurdles in sourcing cheap energy.
Global oil prices spiked due to the US-Iran war and fuel pressures pushed wholesale inflation to 9.92% -> Imported energy becomes more expensive, raising domestic transport and power costs.

Higher global bond yields and slowing cross-border capital flows make investors keep money in domestic markets -> Foreign investors pull money out of developing nations like India, increasing pressure on the rupee.
India's foreign reserves sit strong at $765.9 billion giving 11.1 months of import cover -> This acts as a financial cushion against external shocks.

impacts.rationale: Higher wholesale inflation driven by fuel and power pressures means everyday goods and transport could become costlier for consumers — bad for household budgets.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Spillover from higher global bond yields means the government and eventually banks pay more to borrow, which can lead to costlier home and car loans — bad for borrowers.
As global interest rates stay high and capital flows slow down away from developing nations, the rupee can weaken, making imported items like electronics and oil more expensive.
Conflicts in West Asia disrupting energy markets and trade routes push up fuel costs, directly hurting common citizens at the petrol pump.

watch_next: Updates on whether the US implements the 100% tariff threats from the Lindsey Graham Bill against Russian oil buyers.
Further movements in global crude oil prices driven by West Asian tensions.
analysis.caveats: If global energy markets stabilize faster than expected, some of the inflationary pressures on fuel and imported goods could ease.

analysis.tldr: Global pressures from the US could weaken our currency and squeeze stock investments, making everyday imported goods costlier for regular people.
the_story: Ankita Pathak of Ionic Asset notes that the US Federal Reserve (the US central bank) is entering a tightening cycle (raising interest rates or keeping them high to fight inflation).

India faces a tougher monetary policy trade-off (a difficult choice between keeping interest rates low to help growth or high to protect the currency) as the rupee remains under pressure and inflation (rising prices of everyday goods) shows signs of broadening.
Elevated US yields (higher returns paid by US government bonds) and a stronger dollar may weigh on Indian equities (stocks) and capital flows (money moving in and out of the country).
analysis.what_happened: Experts warn that as the US central bank keeps borrowing costs high, global money flows back to America for better, safer returns. This puts pressure on India's currency and narrows the Reserve Bank of India's flexibility to manage local interest rates.
analysis.analogy: It is like a bigger, more popular shop next door raising its daily wages, causing workers to leave your local shop for better pay, leaving you struggling to keep things running.
why_it_matters_india: US Federal Reserve enters a tightening cycle -> US yields and the US dollar strengthen.
Global investors chase higher returns in the US -> money flows out of Indian markets.
Fewer foreign dollars in India -> the rupee weakens (each rupee buys fewer dollars), making imports like crude oil expensive.
Persistent inflation and a weaker currency limit the RBI's ability to cut interest rates, keeping loan EMIs high for borrowers.

impacts.rationale: A stronger US dollar causes the rupee to drop, which is bad for common people because it makes imported goods, travel, and crude oil pricier.
Foreign investors pulling money out to chase higher US yields puts downward pressure on Indian stocks, which can hurt retail investor portfolios.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Global tightening pushes domestic borrowing costs up, which can eventually mean costlier loans for companies and individuals.

watch_next: Statements from the US Federal Reserve on future interest rate decisions
Movement of foreign investor money out of or into Indian stock exchanges

events.headline: Middle East Oil Exports Stage a Remarkable Comeback

items.title: Middle East Oil Exports Stage a Remarkable Comeback
items.summary: Exports of crude oil from the Middle East hit their highest level in September since the war with Iran began, reinforcing a trend of increased supplies despite Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, according to analysis of shipping and commodity market data by industry observers. But while crude levels have risen, the refinery bottleneck that has caused a global spike in diesel prices persists. European Union figures published on October 1 showed diesel pump prices at record levels. Prices have also surged in the United States despite…

events.article_text:
Brent Holds Above $102 as Gulf Export Rebound Offsets U.S. Military Moves

RFE/RL journalists report the news in 21 countries where a free press is banned by the government or not fully established. We provide what many…

Exports of crude oil from the Middle East hit their highest level in September since the war with Iran began, reinforcing a trend of increased supplies despite Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, according to analysis of shipping and commodity market data by industry observers.

But while crude levels have risen, the refinery bottleneck that has caused a global spike in diesel prices persists. European Union figures published on October 1 showed diesel pump prices at record levels. Prices have also surged in the United States despite the recovery in oil exports.

"More oil is coming out of the Middle East Gulf than many expected that would be possible even just a few months ago," Richard Meade, chief editor of Lloyds List, told an online briefing on October 1.

Lloyds List data shows a steady upward curve of crude tanker transits through the Strait of Hormuz since mid-July, following a sharp fall that coincided with the collapse of the US-Iran memorandum of understanding aimed at ending the conflict, now in its eighth month.

Investment bank JP Morgan said Middle East crude exports in September were at 98 percent of pre-war levels, describing it as "a remarkable recovery for a region still at war."

Commodities analytics firm Kpler reported Saudi oil exports were at average levels for 2025, while maritime intelligence company Windward said Saudi terminals loaded four times more oil than in August -- a big increase but still nearly 40 percent lower than in January.

There appear to be a number of factors behind the revival, including the Saudi East-West oil pipeline, the use of oil shuttles and ship-to-ship oil transfers, and a willingness by some in the industry to accept higher risk.

The Saudi pipeline, which pumps its crude to the Yanbu port on the Red Sea to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, was damaged in an attack by Iran-aligned Houthi militants on September 10. An uptick in shipments from Yanbu later in the month, however, suggested the pipeline had regained at least some of its lost operational capacity.

The United Arab Emirates has found a similar solution, using its pipeline to the port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. It has been targeted in Iranian attacks but is far less vulnerable than Hormuz.

Another route to market has been to use smaller shuttle vessels to transport crude through the Strait of Hormuz, using a route hugging the Omani coastline patrolled by the US Navy. These ships, often traveling in a convoy, pump their cargoes onto tankers in the safety of the Gulf of Oman.

Meanwhile, refineries in India have reportedly begun commissioning tankers to use the route directly.

The risks to shipping have not disappeared. In the latest incident, three Liberian-flagged tankers were struck by unknown projectiles when ‌transiting the Strait of Hormuz on September 30. Industry analysts suggest the dangers have simply been priced in.

"Higher exports do not necessarily mean that the Strait of Hormuz has become safe. They simply show that the oil industry has become accustomed to working around that danger," Meade said.

Crude prices have retreated from recent highs, but refinery bottlenecks remain a global issue. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), much of this is in the Persian Gulf.

Iranian attacks on refineries combined with Hormuz shipping disruption have led to a collapse in output, the IEA said.

"In 2025, Middle East producers exported 3.3 million barrels per day of refined oil products. But since the conflict began, as much as 3 million barrels per day of refining capacity has been unavailable," the IEA wrote in a note on September 21.

This global diesel shortage has been compounded by Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, leading the Kremlin to impose a diesel export ban.

"Refineries around the world are already stretched to capacity," the IEA said. "This leaves few available options to prevent a further tightening of supplies and higher prices in the coming months."

analysis.tldr: A rebound in Middle East oil shipments brings some relief to global crude supplies, but a persistent global diesel shortage means fuel costs remain high for consumers.
the_story: Crude oil exports from the Middle East hit their highest level in September since the war with Iran began, reaching 98 percent of pre-war levels according to JP Morgan.
Data from maritime intelligence firm Windward showed Saudi terminals loaded four times more oil in September compared to August.

Countries and companies bypassed the risky Strait of Hormuz using alternative routes like the Saudi East-West pipeline, the UAE pipeline to Fujairah, and small shuttle vessels protected by the US Navy.

Despite higher crude exports, a severe global diesel shortage persists because refinery capacity has collapsed by as much as 3 million barrels per day in the Persian Gulf and Russian refineries have been hit by Ukrainian attacks.
analysis.what_happened: Middle East oil exports staged a remarkable comeback in September, with shipments bouncing back to near pre-war levels. This happened because oil companies and countries found creative ways to bypass the dangerous Strait of Hormuz—using pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman, and running small ship convoys escorted by the US Navy. Meanwhile, Brent crude held above $102 as these supply increases offset ongoing U.S. military moves.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major highway being blocked by hazards, so delivery trucks instead start using side roads, local ferries, and guarded convoys to get goods through, keeping shelves stocked even if the main route remains dangerous.
why_it_matters_india: Middle East crude oil exports recover and reach 98% of pre-war levels, easing total crude supply shocks.
Indian refineries begin commissioning tankers to use the Omani coastline route directly to keep importing crude.
Global diesel shortages and damaged regional refineries keep fuel and refining bottlenecks high worldwide.
Higher global fuel costs pressure India's import bills and domestic inflation, as India imports the majority of its oil.

impacts.rationale: More oil coming out of the Middle East helps lower crude prices from recent highs — good for lowering import costs.
Persistent global diesel shortages and broken regional refineries keep refined fuel prices high — bad for everyday transport and goods costs.
High diesel and energy costs push up the price of moving goods across the country — bad for household budgets.
Ongoing high energy import bills mean India needs more dollars to pay for fuel, which can weaken the local currency — bad for purchasing power.

watch_next: Updates on the operational capacity of the Saudi East-West pipeline and UAE pipelines
Global diesel inventory levels reported by the International Energy Agency (IEA)
analysis.caveats: Further military escalattacks or sudden closures of alternative pipelines could quickly disrupt these shipping workarounds.

events.headline: America’s Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act reflects much of what’s wrong with today’s war-ravaged world

items.title: America’s Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act reflects much of what’s wrong with today’s war-ravaged world
items.summary: It's a rare case of third parties at risk of penalties for trading with specified countries despite no formal declaration of war against them. India’s oil import needs have put it in a tight spot. While a shift to clean energy is a worthy aim, New Delhi will need to negotiate with the US for now.

events.article_text: Today, on the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, a national holiday but observed perfunctorily in terms of what he stood for, we can only rue the spectacle of a world hell-bent on war. The Graham Act of 2026 passed by both houses of Congress in the United States of America, and signed into law on 18 September, visibly places (without explicitly naming) India in the line of fire for being among the top five importers of Russian crude oil. India stands absurdly implicated thereby for being a financier of the Russian side of the war in Ukraine. Since it is an enabling legislation, the President of the United States is not obliged to act on the powers conferred by the new law to impose tariffs of upto 100% on imports into the US from erring countries, India among them. Internationally, this is a relatively rare instance of a country finding it fit to punish third parties for having trade dealings with countries formally named and targeted in a piece of legislation despite there being no formal declaration of war against them. By implication, Russia and Iran have been designated as forever enemies of the legislating country. During the apartheid era, many countries had trade sanctions against South Africa, but sanctions rarely involved one country punishing a third country for trade dealings with South Africa by levying source-specific tariffs on them. The Graham Act penalizes importers of Russian natural gas differently from Russian crude oil. For natural gas, a floor of 15% of total Russian gas exports has to be crossed before an importing country qualifies for punitive tariffs on its exports to the US. If total exports of Russian natural gas can be increased by finding new buyers, present importing countries above that floor could fall below it without reducing their absolute imports. With crude oil, by contrast, only the rank order in the importer list matters. Crude oil carries no defined floor for punishability in either percentage or absolute terms. The lenience towards natural gas clearly gives an advantage to European buyers of Russian energy, paradoxically favouring countries more vocal in their support for Ukraine. Clearly there were other objectives or biases at play. Of course, crude oil is much the biggest export earner for Russia, between double or triple what the country earns from exports of natural gas. The Graham Act cleared the House of Representatives by a wide margin of 262-159 (14 abstentions), with wide cross-party support. Support for the bill therefore stands at an impressive 60% of the duly elected representatives from a total of 435 Congressional districts. Even though Congressional districts are drawn to give roughly equal demographic representation across all states, it does not necessarily follow that 60% of the people of the US support the bill. Congressional representatives do not always vote according to majority opinion in their respective districts on every issue. There is no international court of appeal. The World Trade Organization is in tatters. The Most Favoured Nation (MFN) principle has now become a sad joke. In any case, international bodies can do nothing to oppose a law passed through due process, even if it seriously overrides international treaties. The office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) will now be in the business of calculating a 12-month moving average of country-wise purchases of oil from Russia to identify the top five purchasers liable under the Act to punitive levies, whether the President chooses to impose a punitive levy or not. And this average will be reassessed every six months. What a comedown for the USTR, once seen as a powerful enforcer of international trade rules. The bite of the Graham Act, if implemented, will be a function of how easily oil importers can find replacement from other sources. What seemed like a possible easing of Iranian restrictions on passage through the Strait of Hormuz, reciprocally with US easing of the naval blockade of Iranian ports, took a jagged turn for the worse on Saturday, 26 September, because of renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia by Houthi rebels in Yemen with alleged Iranian support. Both protagonists in the current phase of the West Asian war are at the mercy of internal dissension. In the US, the forthcoming mid-term elections in the first week of November, and the impact of that on military actions before or after these polls, is completely uncertain at this point. In Iran, a seeming national consensus in support of a diplomatically negotiated peace with the US is snagged on a possibly dissenting faction supporting Houthi rebels in Yemen. For us in India, even if the long-term objective is to move away from oil towards sustainable sources of energy, oil is immediately needed to keep the wheels of the economy turning. The negotiation channel for a bilateral trade deal with the US remains open, and is the only hope for resolution of an impossible situation. The wars underway have been extended by reaction and revenge. Of the many utterances of Mahatma Gandhi on peace, the one most relevant in today’s world is this: “An eye for an eye only ends up making the whole world blind.” Prof. Indira Rajaraman holds a PhD in Economics from Cornell University. She was on the economics faculty at the Indian Institute of Management, Bangalore for 18 years, and subsequently RBI Chair Professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, Delhi. Post-retirement, she was Member of the 13th Finance Commission (2007-2009); and Member for a four-year term (2011-15) of the Central Board of Directors of the Reserve Bank of India. She is on the panel of experts for the Systemic Risk Survey conducted by the RBI for the biannual Financial Stability Report. She has over 70 research publications in peer-reviewed journals and edited volumes and has written a regular column in the Economic Times (2001-04), Business Standard (2010-14) and, currently, Mint (since 2014).

analysis.tldr: A new US law targeting countries that buy Russian oil puts India in the crosshairs, threatening higher trade costs and economic uncertainty.
the_story: The US Congress passed the Graham Act of 2026, signed into law on September 18, which allows the US President to place tariffs (taxes on imports) of up to 100% on countries trading with Russia and Iran.
The law places India in the line of fire because India is among the top five importers of Russian crude oil.
Unlike crude oil, Russian natural gas has a safety floor of 15% of total exports before a country faces penalties, which favors European buyers.
The US Trade Representative will calculate a 12-month moving average of oil purchases from Russia every six months to identify the top five purchasers.
Meanwhile, renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia by Houthi rebels in Yemen on September 26 have complicated global oil supply routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
analysis.what_happened: The US passed a new law called the Graham Act to punish nations that buy energy from Russia and Iran. The law targets top buyers of Russian crude oil, such as India, by giving the US President the power to slap heavy taxes on their exports to America. This comes alongside rising conflicts in West Asia that threaten global oil supplies.
analysis.analogy: It is like a strict school principal passing a rule that punishes any student who hangs out with the school bullies, even if those students just need to buy lunch from them.
why_it_matters_india: India is named as one of the top five importers of Russian crude oil, making it vulnerable to US trade penalties under the Graham Act.
The US trade office will regularly track India's oil buying habits to see if it crosses the threshold for up to 100% tariffs on Indian goods sent to America.
Simultaneously, renewed Middle East conflict risks disrupting oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, threatening energy supplies India needs to keep its economy running.
With international trade rules and groups like the World Trade Organization unable to block this US law, India's main hope lies in its ongoing bilateral trade negotiations with the US.

impacts.rationale: Middle East conflicts and supply threats can push global oil prices higher, leading to costlier fuel for regular people in India.
Trade tensions and potential US tariffs on Indian exports can cause foreign money to leave, weakening the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars), which makes imported goods expensive.
Global geopolitical tensions and war-ravaged news drive investors toward safe assets like gold, making it costlier for Indian buyers.
Fear of US trade penalties and global instability can make stock markets jittery, hurting investor wealth.

watch_next: Whether the US President chooses to actually use the powers granted by the Graham Act to impose tariffs on India
Progress in bilateral trade negotiations between India and the United States
analysis.caveats: Because the Graham Act is enabling legislation, the US President is not legally forced to act on these punitive powers, meaning actual tariffs might never be imposed.

events.headline: Panel to review EU carbon border adjustment mechanism and emissions trading scheme

items.title: Panel to review EU carbon border adjustment mechanism and emissions trading scheme
items.summary: The Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) agreed at its meeting on 25 September to a request from the Russian Federation for the establishment of a panel to review the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) Package and alleged export subsidy under the EU scheme for trading greenhouse gas emission allowances.

events.article_text:
This summary has been prepared by the WTO Secretariat’s Information and External Relations Division to help public understanding about developments in WTO disputes. It is not a legal interpretation of the issues, and it is not intended as a complete account of the issues. These can be found in the reports themselves and in the minutes of the Dispute Settlement Body’s meetings.

The Russian Federation submitted its second request for the establishment of a dispute panel to determine whether the European Union's CBAM and alleged export subsidy under the EU scheme for trading greenhouse gas emission allowances are consistent with the EU's WTO commitments. The EU had objected to Russia's first request for a panel at a DSB meeting on 24 July.

Russia said the CBAM package creates significant trade barriers for covered goods imported into the EU. Russia added that the EU's allocation of allowances to certain companies under the Emissions Trading System (ETS) amounts to an export subsidy intended to strengthen the competitiveness of certain domestic industries.

The EU said it was extraordinary that Russia - which the EU said continues to "wage its war of aggression against Ukraine" - is seeking to rely on international law to improve access for exports into the EU market. The EU said it would take part in the proceedings, not to legitimize Russia's actions, but to reaffirm the EU's strong support for the rules-based multilateral trading system. It also expressed confidence that both the CBAM and the ETS are consistent with WTO rules.

The DSB agreed to the establishment of the panel.

Argentina, Brazil, Canada, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the Republic of Korea, Malaysia, Norway, Paraguay, Singapore, Switzerland, Chinese Taipei, Thailand, the United Kingdom and the United States reserved their third-party rights to participate in the proceedings.

China and Türkiye said they sought to continue engagement with each other for a resolution of this dispute. They requested additional time for the DSB to consider for adoption the panel report circulated on 28 July 2026 in the case initiated by China regarding measures adopted by Türkiye concerning electric vehicles and certain other types of vehicles originating in China.

The parties asked that the DSB further delay consideration of the panel report until 27 October 2026.

Colombia, speaking on behalf of 130 members, introduced for the 100th time the group's proposal to start the selection processes for filling vacancies on the Appellate Body (AB). The extensive number of members submitting the proposal reflects a common interest in the functioning of the Appellate Body and, more generally, in the functioning of the WTO's dispute settlement system, Colombia said.

The United States said that it does not support the proposed decision. The US reiterated that it has set out its fundamental concerns on WTO dispute settlement and that the proposal does not address those concerns. The US stated that, despite efforts by the US and other members in recent years to identify suitable reforms, there remains a wide divergence in views among members regarding the necessary changes.

Over 20 members then took the floor and reiterated their support for the joint proposal and for the urgent need to restore a fully functioning dispute settlement system. Several of the members that took the floor encouraged others to consider taking part in the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA), which provides the possibility of resorting to arbitration under Article 25 of the Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU) in case of an appeal in disputes between any two or more participating members. Several members welcomed Cambodia as the newest member to join the MPIA. The list of current members of the MPIA is available here.

Colombia, on behalf of the 130 members, said it regretted that for the 100th occasion members have not been able to launch the selection processes. Ongoing conversations about reform of the dispute settlement system should not prevent the Appellate Body from continuing to operate fully, and members shall comply with their obligations under the DSU to fill the vacancies as they arise, Colombia said for the group.

The DSB Chair, Ambassador Guilherme de Aguiar Patriota of Brazil, said members' statements at an informal meeting held on 24 July broadly supported information sessions to preserve institutional memory on DS reform. The first information session, held after the DSB meeting on 25 September, consisted of two parts: the first on the history of the DS system, including trends in dispute activity and use of different means of dispute resolution; the second on DS reform processes following the 12th and 13th Ministerial Conferences.

The United States presented status reports with regard to DS184, "US - Anti-Dumping Measures on Certain Hot-Rolled Steel Products from Japan", DS160, "United States - Section 110(5) of US Copyright Act", DS464, "United States - Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Measures on Large Residential Washers from Korea", and DS471, "United States - Certain Methodologies and their Application to Anti-Dumping Proceedings Involving China."

The EU presented it status report with regard to DS600 "European Union and Certain Member States - Certain Measures Concerning Palm Oil and Oil Palm Crop-Based Biofuels" and DS291, "EC - Measures Affecting the Approval and Marketing of Biotech Products" and DS593, "European Union - Certain Measures Concerning Palm Oil and Oil Palm Crop-Based Biofuels."

Indonesia presented its status reports in DS477 and DS478, "Indonesia - Importation of Horticultural Products, Animals and Animal Products."

The next regular DSB meeting will take place on 27 October 2026.

analysis.tldr: A global trade panel review of EU carbon rules could eventually alter compliance costs for Indian exporters selling goods to Europe.
the_story: The Russian Federation submitted its second request for a dispute panel at the WTO to review the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and its Emissions Trading System (ETS).
Russia argues that the CBAM creates trade barriers and that the EU's free allowances under the ETS act as an unfair export subsidy for local industries.
The WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) agreed to establish the panel, with India and 17 other members reserving their third-party rights to join the proceedings.
analysis.what_happened: Russia formally challenged the European Union's new carbon border tax and emissions trading rules at the World Trade Organization, arguing they are unfair trade barriers. Because the EU objected to Russia's first attempt, Russia made a second request, which the WTO Dispute Settlement Body officially approved.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of shopkeepers formally asking a market association to check if the new gate-fee rules set by one dominant shop are fair to everyone else.
why_it_matters_india: India joined the WTO dispute as a third party to protect its export interests against the EU's carbon rules.
The WTO panel will examine whether the EU's carbon tax complies with international trade laws.
If the panel ultimately rules against the EU, it could force Europe to soften carbon compliance costs.
This outcome would ripple through to Indian manufacturing and export sectors that send goods to European markets.

impacts.rationale: Uncertainty over global trade rules can create mild cautiousness in broader markets, which is generally neutral to slightly negative for investor sentiment.

watch_next: Updates from the WTO dispute panel proceedings regarding the EU's carbon border tax
India's official submissions or policy adjustments regarding European carbon compliance
analysis.caveats: This is an early-stage administrative dispute at the WTO, and final panel rulings typically take a very long time to materialize.

analysis.tldr: A weaker rupee makes imported items like crude oil and electronics more expensive for everyday Indians, pushing up daily living costs.
the_story: On Thursday, the Indian rupee dropped to a two-month low against the US dollar.
This drop happened because FPIs (foreign portfolio investors, which are large overseas entities investing in local markets) sold off their Indian investments.
The sell-off was triggered by rising US bond yields (the interest rate the US government pays to borrow) and higher demand for US dollars.
Custodian banks (financial institutions that hold securities for safekeeping) kept buying dollars, showing that money was continuously flowing out of India.
analysis.what_happened: The Indian rupee fell to a two-month low because overseas investors pulled their money out of India. This happened because US bond yields rose, making safe US investments more attractive, which caused global investors to buy more US dollars and sell Indian assets.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local shop losing customers because the shop across the street suddenly started offering a higher interest rate on savings, causing people to pull their cash out and move it there.
why_it_matters_india: US bond yields rise, making American investments look more attractive to global investors.
FPIs (big foreign investors) sell their Indian assets and convert rupees into US dollars.
Higher demand for US dollars causes the rupee to weaken (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
A weaker rupee makes imports like crude oil more expensive, which can increase inflation (the rate at which prices rise) in India.

impacts.rationale: Foreign outflows and high US bond yields put downward pressure on the currency, making imports pricier for regular people.
A weaker rupee raises the cost of imported goods like oil, which usually leads to higher everyday expenses for households.

watch_next: Buying and selling patterns of FPIs (big foreign investors)
analysis.caveats: If foreign investors suddenly change their mind and bring money back into India, the rupee could recover quickly.

events.headline: Crop Care Fed calls for balanced approach to agrochemical use, exports

items.title: Crop Care Fed calls for balanced approach to agrochemical use, exports
items.summary: Union Minister of State for Agriculture and Farmers Welfare Ram Nath Thakur called for responsible use of pesticides and chemical fertilisers

events.article_text:
Ramnath Thakur, Minister of State for Agriculture

The need to balance agricultural productivity with soil health and environmental sustainability, while strengthening India’s agrochemical industry and exports, was emphasised at the 63rd annual general meeting of the Crop Care Federation of India (CCFI).

Union Minister of State for Agriculture and Farmers Welfare Ram Nath Thakur called for responsible use of pesticides and chemical fertilisers, cautioning that excessive application could affect soil quality and human health, according to a statement by CCFI on Thursday.

Thakur also highlighted the government’s efforts to promote natural farming and digital land identification systems to facilitate need-based application of agricultural inputs.

Former Union Environment Minister Prakash Javadekar said climate change posed a major challenge to agriculture and stressed the need for technological innovation and adaptive farming practices, along with a supportive regulatory framework.

Agriculture Commissioner P K Singh said the importance of research and development, climate-resilient crop varieties and safer crop protection products. He stressed the need to address pest resistance and strengthen product traceability and quality standards.

Shivraj Anand, Director & CEO–International Business, Parijat Industries (India), said India needs to move beyond volume-driven competition towards strategic co-development with global innovators to develop safer, lower-dose molecules and biologicals.

“Domestic synthesis of proprietary chemistries can equip farmers with modern, climate-resilient crop protection solutions while strengthening backward integration and export competitiveness,” he said.

Anand called for predictable registration timelines, harmonisation of OECD-GLP data requirements and incentives for green chemistry to help position India as a global hub for sustainable crop protection.

The meeting brought together policymakers, scientists and industry representatives to deliberate on climate challenges, product quality, innovation and export opportunities. Participants stressed greater collaboration among industry, government and scientific institutions to strengthen domestic manufacturing and expand India’s agrochemical exports.

the_story: At the 63rd annual general meeting of the Crop Care Federation of India (CCFI), leaders discussed balancing agricultural productivity, soil health, and exports.
Union Minister of State for Agriculture Ram Nath Thakur warned that excessive pesticide and chemical fertiliser use harms soil quality and human health.
The government is promoting natural farming and digital land identification systems to help farmers use agricultural inputs only when needed.
Parijat Industries Director Shivraj Anand urged India to move beyond volume-driven competition toward co-developing safer, lower-dose molecules and biologicals with global innovators.
analysis.what_happened: Leaders from the government, agriculture departments, and chemical companies met at the CCFI annual general meeting to discuss the future of farming chemicals in India. They debated how to keep crop yields high while protecting the soil and boosting exports, driven by growing challenges from climate change and changing global standards.
analysis.analogy: It is like a farmer trying to balance giving crops enough feed to grow quickly, without overfeeding them so much that it ruins the soil for future years.
why_it_matters_india: The government pushes for digital land identification and need-based farming to reduce chemical overuse.
Agrochemical companies are encouraged to shift toward safer, lower-dose molecules and green chemistry.
Better quality standards and predictable registration timelines aim to boost India's global export competitiveness.
This regulatory focus could change how domestic agrochemical firms manufacture products and manage costs.

impacts.target: Agrochemical company stocks like UPL, PI Industries, and Sumitomo Chemical India
impacts.rationale: Focus on strategic co-development and export competitiveness can benefit strong local chemical manufacturers, which is generally good for investors.
Stronger product traceability and export competitiveness help Indian firms sell more abroad, boosting national trade.

watch_next: New government guidelines on registration timelines for agricultural chemicals
Updates on the rollout of digital land identification systems
analysis.caveats: Government policy changes or stricter environmental regulations could also increase compliance costs for chemical makers if timelines are delayed.

analysis.what_happened: Experts on a policy panel analyzed the political and economic pressures facing Cuba, focusing on U.S. sanctions, energy shortages, and diplomatic relations. analysis.analogy: It is like listening to a town hall meeting about a remote neighborhood's electricity problems — interesting to hear about, but it doesn't change the electricity bill in your own home.
why_it_matters_india: Cuba faces an ongoing energy crisis and U.S. sanctions, as discussed by policy experts.
Cuba and India do not share significant bilateral trade or financial flows that would transmit these events.
Global oil markets remain largely unaffected by Cuban domestic energy struggles since Cuba is not a major global oil supplier.
Therefore, domestic prices, inflation, and financial markets in India experience no direct ripple effects from this specific discussion.

impacts.rationale: No direct link exists between Cuban political discussions and Indian currency markets, meaning the rupee moves based on domestic and broader global factors instead.
Local Indian stocks are driven by corporate earnings and domestic economic policies rather than political panels regarding U.S.-Cuba relations.
Because Cuba's energy crisis does not alter global crude oil supply chains or Indian import costs, consumer prices in India remain untouched.

events.headline: Awkward: Saudi Arabia’s new EV brand takes on the U.S. rival it already controls

items.title: Awkward: Saudi Arabia’s new EV brand takes on the U.S. rival it already controls
items.summary: The Exobot SUV by Ceer Motors

events.article_text:
Saudi Arabia’s first homegrown electric-vehicle maker is set to take on a U.S. rival the kingdom already controls.

Ceer Motors, majority-owned by the sovereign Public Investment Fund, revealed two electric car models on September 21, with deliveries promised for March 2027. The EVs were designed and engineered in Saudi Arabia, and will be built at Ceer’s plant in King Abdullah Economic City, north of Jeddah.

This is the PIF’s third EV bet. It bought about 5% of Tesla in 2018 and sold almost all of it by the end of 2019. It has also put about $8 billion into California-based Lucid, which has never turned a profit.

For the U.S., Ceer’s debut sets up an awkward rivalry: Saudi Arabia is building its own EV brand while its sovereign wealth fund owns a majority stake in Lucid, whose main factory is in Arizona. Ceer is PIF’s hedge against Lucid, whose shares have slumped more than 60% this year and whose Saudi sales are shrinking in a market dominated by China’s BYDiBYDBYD Auto is a Chinese carmaker that became the world’s leading EV manufacturer in 2023, competing with Tesla for market share and global attention.READ MORE.

“Lucid is an existing global technology and luxury-EV company in which Saudi Arabia has invested heavily,” Bill Russo, founder and CEO of Shanghai-based consulting firm Automobility, told Rest of World. “Ceer has a different mandate, creating a Saudi automotive OEM [original equipment manufacturer] and, importantly, an indigenous industrial ecosystem.”

Ceer, a venture between PIF and Taiwanese electronics maker Foxconn, was launched in November 2022. It had set 2025 as the target for its first cars.

Last week, the company’s CEO, James DeLuca, said Ceer will begin production early next year. Ceer has planned more models over the next five years, the company said at the launch. It also aims to make almost half the components of its cars locally by 2034.

Ceer’s Exobot sedan and an SUV are high-powered premium EVs — the segment where Lucid sells its Air luxury sedan and Gravity SUV. The most powerful Exobot versions promise more than 1,100 horsepower, DeLuca said, close to the 1,234 horsepower of Lucid’s fastest car, the Air Sapphire sedan. Ceer has yet to announce prices.

“That does put the initial products closer to Lucid’s premium territory than to BYD’s mass-market center of gravity,” Russo said.

The real test of its strategy will come when that range broadens, Russo said. Lucid, in which PIF holds about 58%, is already badly weakened. This year, it named a new CEO, Silvio Napoli; cut about a fifth of its U.S. workforce; ended its second production shift in Arizona; and recalled 27,000 sedans over a fire risk. Its market value has shrunk to about $1.6 billion.

In Saudi Arabia, Lucid’s sales fell 57% in the first seven months of 2026, while BYD’s rose 369%, according to estimates from Focus2Move, a Rome-based firm that tracks car sales in more than 150 countries. The gap partly reflects price, Hashim AlFatayerji, CEO of the independent Saudi advisory firm Cararak, told Rest of World.

“BYD and Lucid serve very different segments, so comparing their volumes directly can be misleading,” AlFatayerji said.

PIF has kept faith with Lucid through the slump. The carmaker remains one of only five U.S. companies in the fund’s latest quarterly holdings filing, and the Saudi government has agreed to buy up to 100,000 Lucid vehicles over 10 years.

Saudi Arabia has no official count of EV sales. Saudis buy almost 1 million new vehicles a year, and 10,000 to 20,000 of them are electric, AlFatayerji estimated. Joseph Salem, a senior partner who heads travel, transport, and hospitality at consulting firm Arthur D. Little in the Middle East and North Africa, puts the figure at 35,000 to 40,000 EVs in 2025, not counting plug-in hybrids.

Ceer’s factory is designed for as many as 240,000 vehicles a year, and Lucid already runs a smaller plant in the kingdom. That is far more than Saudi buyers can take, Salem told Rest of World.

“Combined, their full-capacity targets are roughly 10 times what the domestic market can plausibly absorb near-term,” he said. “So the majority of output, I’d say 80% plus, has to be export-oriented almost by design.”

Saudi Arabia is building a car industry sized for the Gulf, North Africa, and beyond, backed by PIF money and trade access across the region, Salem said. Exporting is the strategy, he said.

“The domestic market is the proving ground, not the end goal,” Salem said.

60% of the electric cars sold in the Middle East are from China’s BYD.

Abroad, Ceer will meet Chinese rivals that already lead the region. In the Middle East, BYD sells about 60% of electric cars and Tesla about 15%, according to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook.

Chinese carmakers pose a tougher test, Russo said. They have spent years building huge factories, close ties with suppliers, and the ability to sell cheaply, and are now expanding abroad because they can make more cars than China can absorb, he said.

Ceer relies on established suppliers for key parts. Its motors come from Croatia’s Rimac and South Korea’s Hyundai Transys, while its platform is from Taiwan’s Foxconn. It has licensed some component technology from BMW.

“A new entrant cannot simply license its way to that level of competitiveness,” Russo said.

To win buyers at home and abroad, Ceer must match BYD on price, using local parts and state-backed financing, Salem said. It also needs a dealer and service network as wide as BYD’s from the outset, and cars that stand out on their own merits beyond being made in Saudi Arabia, he said.

“It’s a high bar,” Salem said. “But Ceer has the capital and policy backing to close that gap faster than a typical new entrant would.”

Ceer has advantages few new carmakers get, including long-term funding, a powerful backer at home, and the freedom to build on proven technology from others, said Russo. What it still has to earn is a brand that wins customers on

Ceer is majority-owned by Saudi Arabia's sovereign Public Investment Fund and partnered with Taiwanese electronics maker Foxconn.
The new brand creates an awkward rivalry because the Public Investment Fund also owns a 58% majority stake in U.S. electric vehicle maker Lucid.

analysis.analogy: It is like a wealthy landlord who already owns a stake in a struggling foreign restaurant deciding to open a brand-new local kitchen right next door to hedge his bets.
why_it_matters_india: Saudi Arabia pushes to diversify its economy away from crude oil toward manufacturing like electric vehicles.
Increased global competition among electric vehicle makers alters international demand patterns for crude oil and energy.
Shifts in global energy consumption and oil demand impact India's massive crude oil import bills and trade deficit.
Changes in the global auto components and manufacturing ecosystem indirectly influence Indian auto-ancillary and export sectors.

impacts.rationale: Long-term global shifts toward electric vehicles reduce oil demand, which lowers crude prices—generally good for India as a major oil importer.

impacts.target: India's trade deficit (gap between imports and exports)
impacts.rationale: Cheaper energy import costs help narrow the trade deficit, supporting the broader Indian macro economy.

history.title: The day the dollar stopped being gold
history.what: President Nixon went on television on a Sunday evening and announced that the United States would no longer convert dollars into gold for foreign governments. The system that had governed world money since 1944 ended in a fifteen-minute broadcast, and it was never restored.
history.why: Under the Bretton Woods agreement every currency was pegged to the dollar and the dollar was pegged to gold at $35 an ounce. That worked only while America held enough gold to honour the promise. Spending on the Vietnam war and on domestic programmes meant far more dollars circulating abroad than America had gold to back. France and Britain began asking for the gold. The promise was arithmetically impossible to keep, and everyone could see it.
history.impact: Currencies began floating against each other for the first time in modern history, which is why exchange rates move every day now. The dollar fell about a third against major currencies over two years. Gold, freed from its fixed price, went from $35 to $850 by 1980. Inflation across the rich world moved into double digits, because the external discipline that had capped money creation was simply gone.
history.policy: The immediate response was wage and price controls — which failed within two years. The durable answer took another decade: central banks were made independent of elected governments and given an explicit inflation target, so that the discipline gold had imposed from outside was rebuilt inside the institutions instead.
history.consequence: We live in that world now. Money is a promise backed by an institution's credibility rather than by metal, which is precisely why central bank independence is defended so fiercely and why any political interference with a central bank frightens markets so much. It also made currencies a permanent variable in every cross-border investment — the reason a rupee investor has to think about the dollar at all.
history.pattern: When a fixed promise becomes arithmetically impossible, it does not get renegotiated gradually. It gets abandoned suddenly, usually on a weekend, and the people who prepared for the possibility do far better than the ones who trusted the promise because it had always held.
history.india_echo: India's own version came twenty years later, in 1991, for the same underlying reason: a promise the reserves could not fund. Today the echo is quieter but constant — the rupee's long slide against the dollar is the background weather of every Indian portfolio, and it exists because 1971 made currencies float.
history.watch_for: Any peg or price cap that requires ever-larger reserves to defend. Currency pegs, fuel price freezes, and support levels that "will always hold" all end the same way.
